tasks.given: Electroplate the inner surface of a hollow metal object; decide electrode placement.
tasks.independent_solution: For ordinary electrolytic metal deposition, connect the metal object to the negative terminal so its surface is the cathode, and place the anode within the electrolyte-filled cavity facing the desired inner surface without electrical contact with the object. Metal ions in a suitable plating electrolyte are reduced at the cathodic inner wall. If a soluble coating-metal anode is used it can replenish those ions, but a soluble anode is not universally necessary when electrolyte supply is otherwise maintained.
requiredBoundaries: Do not reverse object polarity: an anodic object is not the deposition cathode.
Preserve inner-surface geometry; an anode merely outside does not provide the intended internal current path.
Assume electrolyte access and room for an insulated/separated internal anode rather than an inaccessible sealed cavity.
Do not promise perfectly uniform coating from electrode location alone.
A choice may recognize a complete arrangement, but it cannot prove independent practical layout or construction.

tasks.given: Series-connected electrolytic cells contain the same substance at differing electrolyte concentrations; compare deposited quantities.
tasks.independent_solution: In the ideal Faraday electrolysis model with the same depositing species and charge state and equal current efficiency, the same series current flows through every cell for the same time. Each therefore receives the same charge Q=It and deposits the same mass m=kQ. Different concentration can change the cell's voltage requirement or resistance, but does not give different series charges. Outside this model, differing depletion or side reactions can change useful deposition efficiency, so equal mass is not an unconditional statement for arbitrary real cells.
requiredBoundaries: Retain series connection, common elapsed time and same electrochemical equivalent.
Do not replace constant-current series reasoning with equal-voltage parallel reasoning.
State the ordinary ideal Faraday/equal-efficiency assumption if claiming equal deposition.
No specified concentration ratio or numeric mass may be invented.

tasks.given: During1s positive ions carry charge magnitude3C and negative ions carry charge magnitude2C through a section; find external current.
tasks.independent_solution: Under the ordinary steady electrolysis interpretation, positive and negative ions cross in opposite drift directions. Reversing both charge sign and drift direction makes their conventional-current contributions have the same sign, so the transported-current charge magnitude is3C+2C=5C. I=5C/1s=5A in the external circuit. Subtracting the charge magnitudes would instead confuse net signed charge with charge contributing to through-current.
requiredBoundaries: Both ionic species carry conventional current in the same direction despite opposite particle drift.
Name the ordinary steady opposite-drift model if the visible question adds explicit directional language.
Do not count charge accumulation or unspecified transient displacement current as supplied data.

tasks.given: Contrast electrolyte dissociation with gas ionization.
tasks.independent_solution: Ordinary electrolyte dissociation separates dissolved electrolyte species into mobile positive and negative ions; for an ionic compound dissolution separates existing ionic constituents rather than necessarily stripping electrons into a free-electron population. Gas ionization commonly involves an energetic collision or radiation removing an electron from a neutral atom/molecule, producing a positive ion and a free electron. Subsequent attachment can also form negative gas ions. Thus neither mechanism should be defined simply as every ion losing an electron, and the liquid/gas carrier distinction does not imply that all gas ions are positive.
requiredBoundaries: Do not say electrolyte dissociation necessarily makes only free electrons and positive ions.
Do not say a gas can never contain negative ions.
Preserve separation of electrolyte constituents versus creation of charged gas species/free electrons.
A correct recognition choice does not prove an independently written full comparison.
